name: Garcinia cambogia
lead: Garcinia cambogia, now classified as Garcinia gummi-gutta, is a tropical fruit tree native to the Western Ghats of southwestern India. Its dried rind is a sour flavouring in curries, and its principal acid, hydroxycitric acid (HCA), is extracted and sold as a dietary supplement for weight management.[1][2]

People take it to lose body fat and look leaner, with the stated chain being: HCA reduces fat synthesis or appetite, so less fat is stored, which gives a slimmer waist, trimmer midsection and a less puffy face. In laboratory work (-)-HCA inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, and that finding underlies the claim.[3][20] Supplements are sold as capsules, powders and as an ingredient in multi-ingredient fat-burner and appetite-control blends.

The extract became a mass-market product after it was promoted on US television in late 2012.[1][22] A 12-week randomised controlled trial in JAMA tested it for body weight and fat mass, a 2020 meta-analysis of eight trials reported small average reductions in weight, BMI and waist circumference versus placebo, and systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements describe the overall evidence as limited or inconsistent.[4][5][6][7] Cases of liver injury have been reported with products that contained it, notably the multi-ingredient brand Hydroxycut.[1][8][9][21]

paras: Garcinia gummi-gutta is a tree up to about 20 metres tall in the Clusiaceae family, found in the central and southern Western Ghats and growing as an understory tree along streams up to about 1,800 metres. Garcinia cambogia is a former scientific name. Common names include brindle berry, Malabar tamarind, kudam puli on the Malabar Coast and goraka in Tamil-speaking areas of Sri Lanka and India.[1]

Its pumpkin-shaped fruit is used as a souring agent in curries in India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, for example southern Thai kaeng som and the Coorg vinegar kachampuli.[1] The rind turns dark brown or black when dried and cured.[1] Ayurvedic tradition associates sour flavours with digestion, and ethnobotanical uses include remedies for bowel complaints.[1][2]

HCA is the compound most associated with the species, and the fruit also contains polyphenols such as luteolin and kaempferol.[1][3] A 2015 overview in Fitoterapia summarises the chemistry, traditional uses and research on the plant.[2]

In appearance communities and the wider supplement market, Garcinia cambogia is used as a fat-loss and appetite-control aid, typically alongside diet and training and often inside blended products with other ingredients such as green tea, forskolin or caffeine. Users aim for a leaner midsection and lower overall body fat, which also changes how defined the jaw and face look at lower body-fat levels.

On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, it appears in decades of threads about fat burners, appetite suppressants and carb blockers, with some posters describing it as an appetite suppressant and others listing it among supplements that were each billed as the next big thing.[23][24] Content aimed at younger or beginner users has recommended it as a fat burner.[25]

(-)-HCA is a competitive inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase, the enzyme that converts citrate to oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA; acetyl-CoA is a building block for fatty acid synthesis, which is why HCA is proposed to reduce fat production.[3][20] Of HCA's four isomers, the (-) form is the one found in Garcinia.[20]

Animal work reported that chronic HCA administration in mice spared carbohydrate use and promoted lipid oxidation during exercise.[10] Proponents also propose that HCA raises satiety through serotonin or glycogen-related signalling. A 2000 randomised study in 89 mildly overweight women tested the appetite hypothesis directly and reported no effect of HCA on appetitive variables.[11]

The 1998 JAMA trial randomised 135 overweight adults to 1500 mg of HCA per day or placebo for 12 weeks alongside a high-fibre, low-energy diet. Both groups lost weight, with mean loss of 3.2 kg on HCA and 4.1 kg on placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant, and fat mass change also did not differ; the authors concluded that it failed to produce loss beyond placebo.[4] The paper is the one most often cited in media coverage and forum discussion of the supplement.[22][26]

A 2000 study in 89 mildly overweight women on 5020-kJ diets found that the active group lost 3.7 kg versus 2.4 kg for placebo, a significantly greater reduction, but no effect on appetite.[11] A 2020 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of eight trials with 530 participants reported that Garcinia cambogia reduced weight by 1.34 kg, BMI by 0.99 kg/m2, fat mass percentage by 0.42 percentage points and waist circumference by 4.16 cm relative to placebo, with a nonlinear dose-response relationship for weight and BMI.[5]

Other reviews of dietary supplements and herbal medicines for obesity describe the evidence as limited, weak or inconsistent.[6][7][12] A 2014 randomised trial reported a lipid-lowering effect in obese women,[13] and a 2008 controlled trial examined serum sex hormones in overweight subjects.[14] In the media coverage of the 2014 Senate hearing, a 2013 meta-analysis was described as saying that benefits remained to be proven in larger, longer trials.[22]

Reported effects include dry mouth, nausea, stomach discomfort and headache, and a 2011 meta-analysis found gastrointestinal events about twice as common as with placebo.[1][20] HCA is described as contraindicated in people with colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, and reference works note possible interactions with diabetes, asthma and clotting medicines.[1][20]

Liver toxicity has been reported with Hydroxycut, a brand whose pre-2009 formulas contained HCA among other ingredients. In May 2009 the FDA advised consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products, citing 23 reports of serious problems including at least one death, and the manufacturer voluntarily recalled the products; the reformulated line retained only caffeine from earlier versions.[21] Because those formulas were mixtures, attributing injury to a single ingredient is difficult. A 2022 case report describes a supplement-related liver injury with Garcinia cambogia, tabulations and a systematic review of herb-induced liver injury list Garcinia-containing products, and a 2024 review concluded that HCA-containing foods and supplements may cause liver disease.[8][9][15][20] A systematic review has also examined adverse events of herbal weight-loss supplements generally.[16]

subs.h: The Dr Oz segment and 2014 Senate hearing
paras: In a November 2012 episode, US television host Mehmet Oz described Garcinia cambogia as a revolutionary fat buster, and Wikipedia reports he called it an exciting breakthrough in natural weight loss; his endorsements often lifted sales of featured products.[1][22]

On 17 June 2014 a US Senate consumer-protection subcommittee chaired by Senator Claire McCaskill held a hearing on deceptive weight-loss advertising and questioned Oz about Garcinia cambogia, green coffee extract and raspberry ketone. McCaskill said she did not understand why he needed to say such things when he knew they were not true, according to news coverage; Oz acknowledged using flowery language, said he believed in the products enough to give them to his family and described himself as a cheerleader for viewers who feel hopeless.[22] After the hearing he said he would be more careful about how he discussed products.[22] On T Nation, a 2015 thread reproduced coverage of physicians' call for Columbia University to dismiss Oz, quoting his on-air Garcinia remarks.[27]

Garcinia extracts also appear as ingredients in homeopathic weight-loss products. One US label states its claims are based on traditional homeopathic practice, are not accepted medical evidence and are not FDA evaluated.[17]

In the United States it is sold as a dietary supplement, a category in which products are not approved by the FDA for effectiveness before sale. Multi-ingredient weight-loss products have drawn FDA advisories, such as the 2009 Hydroxycut warning.[21]

Human trials include the 12-week JAMA randomised trial of 1500 mg per day of HCA in 135 overweight adults,[4] the trial in 89 women measuring appetite,[11] a 2014 randomised trial in obese women,[13] a 2008 controlled trial of serum sex hormones,[14] and a 2020 meta-analysis pooling eight trials.[5] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of herbal weight-loss products have also included Garcinia species.[6][7] A 2025 randomised study has examined Garcinia cambogia in lower urinary tract symptoms from prostate enlargement, an unrelated use.[18] Registered trials of related Garcinia species such as mangosteen address weight loss and other conditions.[19]

lore.intro: Garcinia cambogia is discussed in bodybuilding and fat-loss communities as a natural appetite suppressant and fat blocker, and as a recurring example of supplements promoted through television and advertising.[23][24][27]

claims.claim: It blocks fat production in the body.
claims.believers: Proponents point to HCA's inhibition of ATP-citrate lyase and say it stops sugar being turned into fat.[3][20]
claims.experts: The enzyme inhibition is shown in laboratory work; the 1998 JAMA trial found no difference in fat mass versus placebo, while a 2020 meta-analysis found small average reductions.[3][4][5]

claims.believers: Forum posters describe it as an appetite suppressant that has long been used for this purpose.[24][28]
claims.experts: A 2000 randomised study in 89 women found no effect of HCA on appetitive variables.[11]

claims.claim: It is a 'revolutionary fat buster' that works without diet or exercise.
claims.believers: The claim was made on a US television show in 2012, and supplement sellers repeated it.[22]
claims.experts: At a 2014 Senate hearing, a senator criticised the claim; reviews of weight-loss supplements describe limited or inconsistent evidence.[6][7][22]

claims.believers: Users expect a leaner midsection from taking it with diet.[25]
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis of eight trials reported a 4.16 cm average waist reduction versus placebo, with dose-response varying by outcome.[5]

claims.claim: Because it is a natural fruit extract it is safe.
claims.believers: Sellers and users describe it as a natural alternative to stimulant fat burners.[24]
claims.experts: Gastrointestinal effects were about twice as common as placebo in a meta-analysis, and liver injury has been reported with products containing it, including Hydroxycut, which was recalled in 2009.[1][15][21]

claims.claim: It is one of a series of 'next big thing' fat-loss supplements.
claims.believers: Longtime forum members list it with other once-popular supplements that were each promoted as the key to getting lean.[23]
claims.experts: Systematic reviews of dietary supplements for body-weight reduction describe the evidence for such products as weak or inconsistent.[6][12]

card.summary: HCA-based fat-burner supplement; trials and reviews mostly find weak effects, with some liver-injury reports in blended products.
card.aka: Garcinia gummi-gutta, HCA, brindle berry, Malabar tamarind
card.note: Liver toxicity has been reported with multi-ingredient products containing the extract.

quick.overview:
Garcinia cambogia is a tropical fruit whose rind contains hydroxycitric acid (HCA), sold as an over-the-counter weight-loss supplement.

A 1998 JAMA trial and later systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements describe limited or inconsistent evidence of benefit.
quick.mechanism: In the lab, HCA inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme involved in making fatty acids, which is the basis for claims that it reduces fat storage.
quick.risks: Reported effects include nausea, stomach discomfort, headache and dry mouth. Liver toxicity has been reported with products containing the extract, and it may interact with some medicines.
